items.body: Review by Matti — -- The First Review --There is one rather frustrating downside to this compilation: the lack of release years of the source albums. That said, the listened surely would also appreciate some liner notes, too. At least the musicians with their intruments are listed trackwise, as well as composers, and the source albums albeit sadly without the years. Therefor especially for the timeline you are driving blind, so to speak, unless you do online search while listening. I won't be doing that now, so my review concentrates on the musical contents. And they are quite interesting! In general, it seems that most progheads only appreciate/remember Curved Air's early classic era featuring both violinist Darryl Way and keys/guitar player Francis Monkman, ie. the first three albums '70 -' 72. True, the band's later phases, built around vocalist Sonja Kristina, are uneven and a bit messy, but all the more positively this 2-disc set can surprise you. I guess nearly all material here dates from this Millennium, perhaps with some 90's thrown in. Four tracks come from the 2014 Curved Air album North Star which I have given a warm review. The next biggest representation of Curved Air itself is for Reborn (2008). The point of this set, however, is to represent also solo projects of Kristina, Way, Monkman and the numerous musicians who have contributed to the band's later eras. Just too bad there are no liner notes, because this is exactly such release where they would be very useful and valuable. The songs from Reborn actually sound pretty good in their modern production. 'Screw' was a new version of the song from the CA debut Air Conditioning. One track is (prev. unreleased) from the Reborn sessions and another is a Japanese only bonus track. Kristina, Way and the original CA drummer Florian Pilkington-Miksa were accompanied by guitarist Andy Christie.Of solo projects of Darryl Way is here represented Children Of The Cosmos and its fine title track. Monkman's solo harpsichord recording of H�ndel's Suite No. 7 (Ouverture) is among the numerous previously unreleased tracks, like also the Way & Kristina collaboration 'Ichiban Girl'.Bassist Mike Wedgwood sings his own laid-back, blues-flavoured song 'Coming Out'. 'Towards Tomorrow' is a fusiony instrumental from Curved Space which was practically a jam-based brainchild of Monkman and Pilkington-Miksa. 'Shame' is a bluesy vocal track from guitarist Kirby Gregory's solo album. Drummer Stewart Copeland (of The Police fame, and Sonja's husband) offers his previously unreleased piece performed with a symphony orchestra.CD 2 contains several more previously unreleased tracks, and quite nice ones, such as violinist Paul Sax's (and keyboardist Robert Norton's) instrumental 'By the Fire'. 'Moon Beams' is an ethereal, beautiful collaboration of Kristina and Norton, and 'One Step Forward' an elegant instrumental for three bass guitars, by Chris Harris. 'Labyrinth' is a 13-minute instrumental composed by Norton, Pilkington-Miksa and Gregory. Kit Morgan plays all instruments on his Eclectica Historica breezy instrumental piece 'The Gift', and so does drummer Andy Tween on his 'Paraselenae'. The set is closed by Curved Air's lovely Yes tribute 'Soon' where Kristina has rather Jon Anderson -like vocals.All in all, this is a very versatile and pleasant set, and a solid proof of the high level of musical talent that has graced Curved Air's later periods. With proper information and liner notes my 3,5 stars would definitely have been rounded up.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — The Moth by Devin Townsend is one of his most expansive and overall challenging works he has released in the past few years. Mixing his ambient work, with his recent interest in orchestral arrangements and keeping parts of his well known progressive metal and rock style. Very much a full piece, as if it's one long track, it is very formless and not overly accessible, but in many ways it's another great example of the form matching the content, with Devin's lyrics being a rather obtuse description of self discovery, with interesting repetitive phrases and words throughout used that are there more to accompany the music rather than being focused to the plot, which is overall a style Devin has been practicing for a long time. Musically very interesting, with great use of volume and experimental pacing, it's almost like a more musical version of the experimental album The Puzzle he released a few years ago. It's not easy to grasp but you have to respect the overall accomplishment. I'd give this a low 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Home At Night.

items.body: Review by snobb — With their third album, which is unpretentiously titled "III", Italian post-rock quartet Aether confirms they are a rock band first of all. The listener gets a lot of screaming guitars and Fender Rhodes passages, a dose of raw energy, and some nice tunes too. In the fashion of nowadays, all sound is elegantly "electronised." But some nuances make the band's music so special...Getting their inspiration from prog giants "King Crimson", Aether takes one leg stepping into the territory of contemporary jazz, quite successfully combining the best elements of two worlds. "Oort Cloud ", the opener, starts as a bit dreamy ballad, which soon develops into a keys-heavy rock piece with a classic's touch. Complex arrangements don't make the composition overcrowded, though. It ends up the same way as it started - slowly and dreamy. "Vogon" is a different beast, with easily recognizable Claudio Milano vocals. There are a lot of screaming guitar solos and an elegant tune too. "Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres" offers ever-changing rhythmic structures, full-bodied sound, and space-rock aesthetics. "La Mélancolie Du Petit Prince" is a beautiful piano-based song with a touch of melancholy, scented with tasteful electronics. Gorgeous! "Panta Rei" demonstrates excellent interplay among piano, bass, guitars, and flute, as if taken from an "Oregon" jazz band's discography, with the addition of rock energy. "Swerve", the closer and longest album composition (10+ minutes), relies on proggish keyboards and returns the listener to the world of Yes aesthetics. "Aether III" is an excellent answer to those proclaiming that progressive rock has stuck in the 70s. Fortunately, no. The album's music, played by extremely technically skilled musicians, demonstrates that the third decade of the new Millenium still has something to offer - fresh, creative, non-boring, and with a deep respect for the genre's legacy.

items.body: Review by James Lee — I'm in the minority here (not unusual) in that I greatly prefer Klaatu's first album. Having said that, there's no doubt in my mind that Hope is the better PROG album. It's a complete start-to-finish concept album, maintaining Its narrative and its particular symphonic, often almost martial style of rock-adjacent music from beginning to end, albeit with discrete pieces that have their own character. The story is a sort of sci-fi epic with plenty of 60's style peace and love vs oppression and repression themes woven in. There's little of the winking tongue-in-cheek feel of the first album; while these lads don't take themselves so seriously that humor is absent from the mix, there's no overt Rugglesby or Anus of Uranus moments here. 1977 was well before "steampunk" was a genre, but the band's musical and narrative approach on Hope isn't a million miles away from fitting the general retro Victorian in space feel. It's a fun and sometimes genuinely emotive ride that I highly recommend to those of us that can still maintain our attention span for an entire LP. A work of masterful but not demonstrative musicianship, as well as a somewhat poignant glimpse of a time when the 1960s spirit was still strong enough to inspire 1970s bands to baroque statements, before the fashionable and generational fault lines banished such wonderfully over-the-top musical statements to the margins.

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — Today I'll be posting my first review of a progressive electronic record, that record being Integeati Disintegrati by the Italian Franco Leprino. It consists of two long suites called Part One and Part Two, respectively, making the whole album a single forty-minute-long venture through the soundscapes of his creation. Progressive electronic as a genre has always been a mixed thing for me, never quite striking me exactly at the right point to really leave much of an impact on me, but every once and a while it happens, and I would argue that this album falls into that category. It had a more thought-out approach to the material while still remaining free. It's very captivating and brings a sense of hope contrasted to the more moody background of the music, all while remaining in the same piece. Franco Leprino mixes in classical folk and chamber music at points masterfully with his brilliant keyboard arrangements, making use of a wide array of various instruments (mainly played by just him, but also mixing in four other session musicians). The album's opening is this fragile fusion of spacey guitar and mysterious synths, flowing beautifully with each other and remaining engaging with the listener by drawing out the experience while still maintaining a clear (yet minimalist) presence. It really does feel like a dream at points, simply blowing in the wind while keeping its own details hidden to the naked eye, allowing you to reach in and grasp the secrets of the music's world. Later in Part One we get this moody collage of noises, piano, looping guitars and effects, as well as an overall build-up that feels incredibly natural and unique for its time. The finale of Part One is this gorgeous mix of deeply touching synths and oboe as well as more light folk music backing it. Part Two feels a lot more cryptic, droning on various rhythms and riffs for a while before seamlessly fading into the next section. Franco seemed to be way ahead of his time with how one-of-a-kind his music sounds. Avant-garde, yet strikingly dynamic with both lovely and uncanny arrangements seeping into the music here. In conclusion, this was a very enjoyable experience with tons of interesting details to unpack. It feels like almost nothing out of Italy around that time, and it's a shame more people don't know about this one. We can only dream of what Franco could've also made if he hadn't gone to never release music again after this, as I feel like there's no doubt that his name would've started to garner attention in the underground experimental and electronic scenes. This is deserving of a strong 4.25/5 in my eyes.

items.body: As an ardent admirer of Petrenko’s Liverpool Shostakovich cycle (Naxos), I was excited to hear his first Mahler recording for Harmonia Mundi — and it does not disappoint. Symphony No. 3 Amazon Presto Apple In recent years I have reviewed two other performances of this work: the Czech PO under Bychkov (Pentatone – review) and the Minnesota SO under Vänskä (BIS – review). Both feature gorgeous orchestral sound that disguises lackluster interpretations. Both labels provide a deep and wide soundstage, with the largest possible dynamic range in a complementary acoustic that adds a certain homogenous glow to the strings. By comparison, Harmonia Mundi’s live recording, made in the Royal Albert Hall, London, on 27 April 2023, is closely miked, and occasionally sounds constricted: there is an occasional balance issue, and little bloom around the sound. But on repeated hearing the ear adjusts, giving us an opportunity to hear this orchestra playing at the top of its considerable game. Petrenko shapes the first movement with a sure hand, never letting it feel like a series of disjointed episodes. Mahler described this music as “hardly anything but sounds of nature,” a description that surely requires the hyper-expressive performance heard here. The opening implacable horn pronouncement leads to brooding, elemental urgings from the lower instruments; Matthew Gee’s wonderful trombone solo ensures the struggle for life is very much heard and felt. I admire the willingness of the woodwinds to make beauty of execution secondary to vivid characterization: just listen to those squawking piccolos and shrieking E-flat clarinets. Many performances downplay the moments where Mahler asks for different tempos at the same time, but Petrenko and his players positively revel in it (sample the solo violin and horn around 18’20”); the ‘Rabble’ music (right around 21’50”) is truly disorderly. The frenetic Coda marks the end of one of the most exciting readings in recent years. The first movement’s wildness is countered by a second movement of sweet gentleness, played by the Royal Philharmonic with beauty and nuance. The Scherzo (which quotes from Mahler’s early song Ablösung im Sommer / Relief in Summer) is also successful, though I wanted the offstage posthorn (gorgeously played by Toby Street) to be more distant. Is this the conductor’s choice or an engineering issue? Close miking also negates the sense of delicate shimmering in the string accompaniment. The final terror-filled build-up leads to a driven, frenzied climax. Vasily Petrenko. Photo © Bård Gundersen. The two vocal movements are less impressive. Hanna Hipp’s wide vibrato quickly develops a pronounced beat, and she seems unwilling to sing softly. Her generalized somber interpretation is no match for the sensitive expressiveness of Janet Baker (LSO/Tilson Thomas/Sony Classical), Christa Ludwig (NYPO Bernstein/DG), and Birgit Remmert (CBSO/Rattle/Warner Classics). The fifth movement is lustily dispatched (with fabulous orchestral bells), though the joyful excellence of the Tiffin Boys’ Choir is somewhat hampered by the prominent vibrato from the women of the Philharmonia Chorus. And surely with the mics so close, diction should be more emphatic. The final movement’s tempo marking (Langsam, Slow) is rather generic, allowing for a wide variety of timings: Iván Fischer (BFO/Channel) takes 21’31” whereas Tilson Thomas’s second reading (SFSO) takes 26’31”, more than a minute and a half slower than Bernstein’s second New York Philharmonic reading (DG). I find Abbado’s Berlin performance (22’25”, also recorded live in the Royal Festival Hall in 1999) profoundly moving, but Petrenko, taking about a minute longer, runs a close second, with particularly lovely playing from the strings and principal woodwinds. Towards the end of the Noch etwas bewegter (9’20”), a greater accelerando may have caught more of the pained intensity Abbado and Bernstein find. But Petrenko is careful to keep the brass as delicate coloring through most of the movement, so that when they finally are unleashed in the Coda the sound gains a new powerful radiance that is deeply moving. Bruno Walter described this movement as “a single sound of heartfelt and exalted feelings, in which the whole giant structure finds its culmination.” Certainly, that is true here. Harmonia Mundi’s booklet includes a written introduction by the conductor, fine notes by Dr. Genevieve Robyn Arkle, texts, and translations, as well as the rosters of the orchestra and choirs. I do hope that Petrenko and Harmonia Mundi plan on more Mahler releases (there has been positive press for recent performances of the first and eighth symphonies) — warmly recommended. Recommended Comparisons Mahler: Symphony No. 3 Leonard Bernstein | Claudio Abbado | Michael Tilson Thomas | Jonathan Nott The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: Industrial solo artist Staytus, the project of Sam Grundemann, has signed with the US label Cleopatra Records last month and now released the digital single and video “S + M” on May 29, 2026. The single is the first announced collaboration between Grundemann and Cleopatra Records. Musically “S + M” mixes industrial, electronic and nu-metal elements. Thematically the track deals with separation, unresolved emotional connection and the idea of reunion within a “twin flame” relationship. “This song lives in that space between losing someone and never fully letting them go,” Grundemann adds. “It’s about the kind of connection that doesn’t just end—it lingers, evolves and keeps calling you back. Signing with Cleopatra Records felt natural because they’ve always embraced music that carries that kind of emotional weight.” “S + M” is accompanied by a video which was directed by Vicente Cordero of Industrialism Films known for his work for acts including Skold and Stabbing Westward. About Staytus Staytus is the solo project of Sam Grundemann, an Arizona-born musician, producer, songwriter and audio engineer now working from the Los Angeles area. Staytus began as “a personal project” and musically blends industrial, electronic and nu-metal elements. We first covered the project in March 2022 when the project released three tracks from the debut album “Disease Of The Mind”. The debut album “Disease Of The Mind” was released digitally on September 9, 2022 and contains 13 tracks. Staytus followed it with “Wasteland Of Broken Hearts”, released on October 27, 2023 as an 11-track digital album. In 2025, Staytus released several standalone singles and film-linked tracks. We covered “How To Be A Serial Killer“, the closing track in the “Twisted Frames” series, followed by “Headache“, “Heart Attack“, “Kiss N Tell” and “The God, The Artist, & The Creator“. Those releases involved collaborators including Matt McJunkins, Sean Beavan, Mikal Blue, Jeff Friedl, Anthony Laurie and Patrick “Embryo” Tapu.

items.body: The Slovak electro and minimal-wave project ImiAFan – aka 4mg Records founder Imrich Végh – has released a digital EP, “Elmúlt idő” (Passed Time), on Bandcamp, with a wider streaming release scheduled for early June. The EP pairs the original title track with a set of remixes. Alongside the original title track – first issued at the end of 2025 – the EP features remixes by Bornia (Andy Dufter, ex-Staatseinde), Hadron Lundgren (Budapest) and Keen K (Berlin electro/italo), plus a MANASYt “Bigfoot Mix” of the older track “Stupaj.” The lyrics draw on a four-line fragment by Szenes Iván, taken from Kovács Kati’s landmark Hungarian electronic track “Kérdés önmagamhoz” from 1980. Elmúlt idő by ImiAFan About ImiAFan ImiAFan is a Slovak electro, synth-pop and minimal-wave project led by Imrich Végh, active since around 1999–2000. The project describes itself as an “electro / synth-pop project producing probably the most microscopic hits based and forgotten in Slovakia.” Long-time collaborator Miki Bernáth (of Damolh33) handles mixing and mastering, while Végh also runs the 4mg Records label. Side-Line has covered the band on several occasions, including a 2019 “Click Interview” with ImiAFan vs. 4mg Records, in which Végh described himself as “more like a music activist,” and a 2019 report on the project’s 12-inch release via Falco Invernale Records. The project also appeared in Side-Line’s coverage of the Synth Slovakia 2017 compilation. The new digital EP, “Elmúlt idő” (Passed Time), was self-released via Bandcamp on May 29, 2026. About 4mg Records 4mg Records is a dedicated non-profit underground music label, founded in 2003 in St. Catharines, Canada, by electronic musician Imrich Végh (aka ImiAFan). The label underwent a major geographic shift when it relocated to Slovakia in 2006. Operating out of Central Europe ever since, the imprint focuses on cultivating a tight-knit international network of underground artists, prioritizing artistic expression and cultural connection over commercial success. Sonically, the label explores the darker and more experimental corners of electronic music, with a catalog deeply rooted in minimal synth, darkwave, ambient, and industrial sounds. 4mg Records has become a trusted home for both emerging acts and seasoned veterans of the avant-garde scene, featuring releases and collaborations with iconic names like The Legendary Pink Dots, Edward Ka-Spel, Isobutane, and Click Click. Their curated compilation projects, such as the Wave Earplug series, are wellknown for showcasing diverse, global underground talent. 4mg Records bypasses mainstream distribution models to focus heavily on tangible, collectible formats. The label routinely presses music onto high-quality vinyl, cassettes, and limited-edition compact discs. Some of the band’s best-known releases include: Albums & cassettes Edward Ka-Spel – A Carrington Event (2024): A highly sought-after cassette album from the iconic frontman of The Legendary Pink Dots, delivering trademark psychedelic and avant-garde ambient textures. The Legendary Pink Dots – Live At The Rave Milwaukee 20 June 2000 (2025): A curated archival live concert release preserved on limited-edition cassette for collectors of industrial and experimental music. IMIAFAN – Clearly Defined (2024): A minimal-synth and hardware-driven electronic LP from the label’s founder, Imrich Végh. Isobutane – – to 0: A release from Slovak electronic producer Isobutane, exploring intricate IDM and ambient landscapes. Click Click – Gelsenkirchen 1997: A documentation of the historic UK EBM/industrial band’s raw electronic energy. Compilations Wave Earplug Series (e.g., Wave Earplug No. 7): The flagship vinyl compilation series from the label, showcasing an international roster of artists spanning raw electro, synthwave, darkwave, and pumping acid sounds. items.body: Los Angeles deathrock band Ex-VoTo has released “Laodicea,” an eight-track EP on their own Poor Alice Music label in an ultra-limited pressing of 100 copies each on vinyl and CD. The release combines four new studio recordings with rare and previously compilation-only material, including covers of Bauhaus and Siouxsie and the Banshees. Side A collects four new studio recordings: “Angel,” “Fear Me,” “I Want to Stop,” and “Say Goodbye.” Side B features “Emmanuelle,” “Resurrection Mary,” a cover of Bauhaus’s “Slice of Life,” and a cover of Siouxsie and the Banshees’s “Monitor.” “Slice of Life” appeared on Bauhaus’s 1981 album Mask. “Monitor” appeared on Siouxsie and the Banshees’s 1978 debut album The Scream. The new EP follows the release of the anthology “Don’t Look Back (1982–1990)” on Phantom Chord. The anthology compiled songs from Ex-VoTo’s original 1990 “Don’t Look Back” EP alongside rare recordings from the 1982–1990 period that had not previously seen official release. The original “Don’t Look Back” 12″ EP was issued in 1990 on Poor Alice Music and New World Records, pressed on translucent blue, purple, and black vinyl, and recorded at Poor Alice Studios in Garden Grove, California. Ex-VoTo ‘Laodicea’ California tour dates, June 2026 To mark the release, Ex-VoTo plays three California dates beginning June 5, 2026. June 5, 2026 – Queen Bee’s, San Diego, CA – Supporting Kommunity FK, with The Exile and Nervous Gender (Re-Loaded). June 6, 2026 – Klub Terminal at La Santa, Santa Ana, CA – Supporting Kommunity FK, with Gitane Demone + Paul Roessler and Ravens Moreland. The press release lists this show as Los Angeles; a confirmed ticket listing places the venue at 220 E. 3rd St. (Basement), Santa Ana, California — Orange County, not the city of Los Angeles. June 7, 2026 – Club Gallows, Los Angeles, CA – Ex-VoTo headlines, with Pilgrims, In A Darkened Room, Funeral Process, and Bizarron. About Ex-VoTo Ex-VoTo was formed in 1982 in Los Angeles by Larry Rainwater, David Rhine, and Linda Patti. Based initially in Orange County – where the prevailing scene was still dominated by punk rock – the band relocated to Los Angeles to build a following. Their early sound combined drum machines, synthesizers, and heavy guitars at a time when live drummers were the norm, drawing audience friction and, from fellow Deathrock bands, recognition. In 1988, the track “Falling Apart” appeared on Bomp! Records’ “American Gothic: The Krypt Kompilation”, a compilation featuring bands from Los Angeles’s gothic club The Krypt. The placement brought the band to the attention of New World Records and XXX Records. The result was “Don’t Look Back” (1990), Ex-VoTo’s first official vinyl release, a four-track 12″ EP recorded at Poor Alice Studios in Garden Grove and co-released by Poor Alice Music – the band’s own label, which Rainwater has operated independently since then – and New World Records. Throughout the 1990s, Ex-VoTo contributed tracks to several Cleopatra Records gothic compilations, including “The Goth Box”. “Anno Domini” (1995) collected studio versions of their earliest songs, including “Falling Apart” and “If I Never.” “The Light of Day” (2003) moved toward a darkwave electro direction. “Doloroso” (2006) returned to a guitar-driven deathrock approach, and “Antioch” (2009) was the first album Rainwater set out to write as a unified work rather than a collection of individual songs. The band relocated from Los Angeles to New Orleans, and subsequently to Houston following Hurricane Katrina. The core of the lineup has remained Rainwater on bass and lead vocals, and Linda Patti on keyboards and backing vocals. The current lineup adds Heather “Spleen” Rainwater on keyboards and backing vocals and Patrick Midnite on guitar and backing vocals. “Laodicea” is their first new recorded release since “Antioch” (2009), seventeen years on.

items.body: Australian musicians David Thrussell and Darrin Verhagen, working together as David Thrussell & Shinjuku Thief, release “The Call of Cthulhu” on June 19, 2026 via Metropolis Records. The spoken-word album is a retelling of H. P. Lovecraft’s 1928 short story, issued as a deluxe 2xLP, with a digital edition to follow. The album sets Lovecraft’s story to a soundtrack, narrated by Thrussell with music by Verhagen. It follows the structure of the original text in three parts: “The Horror in Clay,” “The Tale of Inspector Legrasse” and “The Madness from the Sea.” Thrussell has worked with Lovecraft source material before: in 2025 he released a Lovecraft-themed record with Flint Glass on Ant-Zen, as reported by Side-Line. “The Call of Cthulhu” is released as a deluxe 2xLP on “crushed bone” colour vinyl, with original artwork by Richard Grant (I+T=R). A digital release will follow, with no date confirmed for it at the time of writing. About H. P. Lovecraft’s ‘The Call of Cthulhu’ “The Call of Cthulhu” by H.P. Lovecraft is a 1928 horror story that pioneered “cosmic horror”. It follows an investigator piecing together clues about a terrifying, ancient, octopus-dragon-human hybrid entity and its global cult, exploring the psychological devastation of humanity when confronted with unimaginable, alien powers. The story is told as a nested mystery through the notes of Francis Wayland Thurston, and is broken into three main parts: 1. The Horror in ClayThe story opens in 1926 with Thurston investigating the estate of his late great-uncle. He discovers a bas-relief sculpture created by a local artist named Henry Wilcox. The sculpture depicts a grotesque, tentacled monster that Wilcox made while experiencing feverish dreams of cyclopean cities and monstrous monoliths. Thurston connects this artifact to similar strange reports and ancient voodoo cults, discovering that people around the world are sharing nightmares about this being: Cthulhu. 2. The Swamp CultThurston learns about a New Orleans police raid on an isolated, swamp-dwelling cult in 1907. The police uncovered horrifying rituals and human sacrifices. The cultists worshipped “The Great Old Ones,” ancient, alien beings who ruled the earth ages ago and are now sleeping beneath the sea. They chant the infamous phrase: “In his house at R’lyeh, dead Cthulhu waits dreaming.” 3. The Sunken City and the SeaThe narrative shifts to a manuscript written by a Norwegian sailor, Gustaf Johansen. Months earlier, his ship was chased and attacked by a mysterious vessel. Johansen and his surviving crew landed on a bizarre, uncharted volcanic island in the South Pacific. They unwittingly discovered the sunken, geometric nightmare-city of R’lyeh. After stepping on the island, they accidentally awakened Cthulhu. The entity slaughtered the crew before Johansen managed to ram Cthulhu with his ship, temporarily breaking apart the creature’s formless, regenerating body long enough to escape. About David Thrussell & Shinjuku Thief David Thrussell is an Australian musician and composer based in Melbourne. He co-founded the industrial and electronic project Snog in 1989 with Tim McGrath and Julia Bourke, and went on to run the related projects Black Lung, formed in 1994, and Soma. Shinjuku Thief is the project of Australian musician and soundtrack composer Darrin Verhagen. It began in 1992 as a trio of Verhagen with Charles Tétaz and François Tétaz, taking its name from Nagisa Oshima’s film “Diary of a Shinjuku Thief,” and worked in a dark ambient and cinematic style, with several records conceived as soundtracks to imagined films. Verhagen released much of the project’s catalogue on his own Dorobo label and later through Projekt, alongside work for theatre, dance and film and a teaching post at RMIT University. “The Call of Cthulhu” is the first release credited to David Thrussell & Shinjuku Thief.

items.body: hackedepicciotto – the duo of Alexander Hacke and Danielle de Picciotto – release the album “Lichtung” on July 10, 2026, via Mute Records, on CD and limited candy-colour vinyl. The hackedepicciotto “Lichtung” album is the duo’s first collection to be sung entirely in German, and follows “The Silver Threshold” (2021). A new track and video for “Zeitenwende,” the fifth track on the record, is now available. “Lichtung” – German for “clearing” – takes its name from the home the duo established on the outskirts of Berlin after fourteen years of nomadic life. Hacke and de Picciotto have described the album as marking a departure from repetitive drone-based approaches in favour of more complex sound structures and electronic terrain. The album is the duo’s most extensive use of the German language to date. The full tracklist is: 1. “Lichtung” 2. “Vogelfrei” 3. “Wiederbelebung” 4. “Erntedank” 5. “Zeitenwende” 6. “Draussen” 7. “Einig” 8. “Der Marschall.” A video for “Wiederbelebung” was released in March 2026 ahead of the album announcement. hackedepicciotto tour dates 2026-2027 hackedepicciotto have announced a number of live dates to accompany the release, including June 27, 2026, at silent green Kulturquartier in Berlin (with Sonic Morgue), and July 10 and 11 in Portugal – Porto at KISMIF Museum of Science and Lisbon at Galeria Zé dos Bois. Below are all of the dates. 6 June – Frankfurt (DE), Ono 10 June – Regensburg (DE), Ostentor Kino 13 June – Düsseldorf (DE), Art:Walk Festival, Weltkunstzimmer 27 June – Berlin (DE), Silent Green – a celebration of LICHTUNG 10 July – Porto (PT), KISMIF Museum Of Science Of Porto 27 Aug – Poznan (PL), Estrada w Centrum 1 Sep – Geneva (CH), Cave 12 Festival la Bâtie – NEW DATE 12 Sep – Den Bosch (NL), William Twee – NEW DATE 15 Sep – Prague (CZ), Archa – NEW DATE 16 Sep – Brno (CZ), Kabinet Mu – NEW DATE 20 Nov – Amsterdam (NL), OCCI – NEW DATE 27 Nov – Sofia (BG), Club Pave – NEW DATE 30 Jan 2027 – Lübeck (DE), Treibsand About hackedepicciotto hackedepicciotto is the project of Alexander Hacke and Danielle de Picciotto, partners in life and work. Hacke is a founding member of Berlin industrial act Einstürzende Neubauten and a contributor to numerous projects over four decades, including Crime and the City Solution. De Picciotto co-founded Berlin’s Love Parade in 1989 and has released extensive solo work as a musician, visual artist and author; she also performed with Space Cowboys and the later incarnation of Crime and the City Solution. The duo began presenting work as hackedepicciotto in the 2010s and released “Menetekel” as a 2LP in 2017. Side-Line covered the announcement of “The Silver Threshold” in August 2021 and the accompanying video for “Kirchhain” in November 2021; “The Silver Threshold” was released November 12, 2021, on Mute, and stands as the duo’s most orchestrally arranged record to date. Side-Line also covered the announcement of three reissues on Mute in 2023 and the release of their first live album in 2024. “Lichtung,” out July 10, 2026, is their first studio album since “The Silver Threshold.”

items.body:
STROOM fills in a gap on the timeline, excavating vital experiments made in Cologne in the wake of the cult 'Novaya Scena' compilation by Svitlana Nianio, Michael Springer, Guido Erfen, Soloveyka, Yewgeny Taran and Wolfram Burgtorf.

Back in 1993, a bizarre 20-track compilation appeared from Cologne's musical fringe. The idea for the set had come from artist and producer Erfen and sound engineer and percussionist Springer, two close friends who, taking advantage of cheap rent and disused buildings, put on regular events and established a recording studio in their neighborhood, off the beaten track. Erfen was a dedicated tape trader and had received a transmission from Kharkiv's Novaya Scena rock club that arrived with an essay and music from three local bands. At this time, Ukraine was still under Soviet rule and the music fascinated the two friends, shining a spotlight on a part of the world they were completely unfamiliar with. When singer and keyboardist Soloveyka visited cologne a year later, she handed Erfan more tantalizing music, inspiring him to make his own pilgrimage to Ukraine to investigate further. The research resulted in the 'Novaya Scene' CD, a set of tracks recorded between 1986 and 1992 that muddled prog with new wave, punk, folk and avant-garde rock. It was released on Hamburg's What's So Funny About label and was supposed to have a sequel.

That's where 'Aftermath and Transitions' comes in. Following the release of 'Novaya Scena', Erfen and Springer set up a series of sessions at their studio, inviting some of the Ukrainian artists to record with them. It's this period that resulted in Svitlana Nianio's 'Transilvania Smile' soundtrack that was properly released for the first time on Muscat sublabel Shukai in 2023. Nianio had been a member of Cukor Bila Smerť (the band who'd provided the stylistic anchor for 'Novaya Scena') and took the opportunity to launch her solo career, with Springer working as engineer. And there was more material from those sessions that Springer held back: the compilation's first four tracks are collaborations between Nianio, Springer, Taran and Springer's good friend Burgtorf. Opener 'Fake' was almost finished when Nianio showed up at the studio with her Casio in tow, so Springer plugged her in and she ended up lavishing the beat with vocals in Ukrainian and oddball keyboard vamps. The other three tracks were a little more organic, improvised in the studio while the artists got familiar with one another - there's the decelerated reggae experiment 'ManySpace', the instrumental groover 'Quiet Place' and best of all 'Політ Світляки', a wiry percussive jam that's not aged a day.

Erfen joins in on the ace exotica-tinged 'Whispering Walls' and 'Tired River', tracks from the group's final session in 1995. Nianio and Taran were planning to renew their visas and return to Cologne to record more, but it never happened - the recordings were shelved and the artists went about their lives independently. Then there's the three Solar tracks recorded by Soloveyka and Burgtorf who struck up a friendship after meeting at Springer's studio. Singing in Russian and English, Soloveyka breathes cabaret energy over Burgtorf's jerky, sample-heavy ethno-groove productions. And it's left to Taran to finish things off, with a "1996 Version" of his 'Death and the Bachelor' track that features none other than Nianio on keys. Phew. It's a brilliant set, really - not just one for STROOM obsessives, it'll speak to anyone whose interest in the Ukrainian underground was piqued by 'Transilvania Smile' or Muscut's ace Cukor Bila Smerť anthology.

items.body:
Constructed in a vacuum from naked FM synth sounds and discreet concrète elements, 'Clock In, Clock Out' is a set of atemporal experiments that exist in their own ecosystem - essential listening if you're into Motion Graphics or Visible Cloaks' enduringly influential 'Fairlights, Mallets and Bamboo' mix.

Xavier García Bardón and Emmanuel Gonay's second release following 2021's brief Lexi Discs 7" 'Aταραξία / Καταστροφή', 'Clock In, Clock Out' sounds reactionary in its own way, completely eschewing current production norms to lock into an airless atmosphere that's at odds with established logic. It makes the record captivating to listen to; there's no real density, very little (if any) reverb, almost no digital processing. As far as we can tell, it's just percussive synth sounds, silence, acoustic drums and a handful of other sounds that seem to fit Bardón and Gonay's methodology. The context appears to be revealed on 'Endnotes', the record's final track, when slow renaissance-era lute strings are plucked to shadow the synthesised sounds we've already heard on the previous tracks. A bell chimes and city sounds leak into the duo's hermetically sealed chamber and it feels unsettling. Going back to the beginning and listening all over again, the unsettlingly artificial sounds begin to make even more sense.

Bardón and Gonay don't make modern early music or nostalgic synth gear, they make sounds that exist on their own timeline. The metronome that they reference in the title is marking years as much as it's marking tempo. Are we listening to the early '80s when we hear FM sounds that Paddy Kingsland and Peter Howell might well have used when they were holed up in the BBC Radiophonic Workshop's windowless studio? Or beamed to the decade's close when the duo recycle the E-mu Emulator II 'Loon Garden' sample that 808 State famously used on 'Pacific State'. It's more complicated than that; the phrases themselves sound older, more ancestral and they're interrupted by seemingly human outbursts that Musica Mosaica sample and distort. Each track seems to exist in the same unsettling uncanny valley, 'Tempistica Metronomica' welding together a web of percussive sounds into glassy a-rhythmic glissando slides and 'Concaténations' sounding like an orchestra virtual bottles being blown by clockwork automatons. 

It's over far too quickly, but it's one of the weirdest, most perfectly self-contained sets we've heard in ages. Huge recommendation.

items.body:
Booting off the new year with his most urgent set in years, Shackleton follows his flawless run of psychedelic future-ancient excursions with a lissom body of left-foot-fwd bangers chiseled specifically for the soundsystem.

If you've only tuned into Sam Shackleton's latter-day material - those s-tier collaborations with Heather Leigh, Marlene Ribeiro, Holy Tongue and Six Organs of Admittance, or even his jaw-dropping 2023 solo tome 'The Scandal of Time' - you can be forgiven for ignoring his earlier, sticker gear, the foundational bass variations that proposed a parallel course for dubstep and his destructive work with scene architects like Pinch, Appleblim and T++. On 'Euphoria Bound', he applies the skills and philosophies he's refined over the last few years traversing the outer perimeters of prog, psych folk and Carnatic music to the dancefloor, re-examining and rethinking his approach without sacrificing any of the thrust. These aren't winding, side-long lattices of rhythm and prismatic, xenharmonic animation, they're taut, shockingly direct bass variations that transmit the same uncompromising message.

There's not a dull moment here, but the best early example might be 'Crushing Realities', a concertinad six-minute marvel that seems to distill so much of Shackleton's most vital elements. He almost sounds as if he's remixing his own body of work, carving into dusty, microtonally skewed vocal snippets and zither chimes with rounded, woody syncopations that split the difference between Midori Takada and Peverelist. But it's not a single element that gives this one its signature; Shackleton's blotter-assisted fractal pattern of tape stop effects, vanishing voices, rhythmelodic sequences and battered radio static is only strengthened by the neck snapping flurry of kicks and undulating basslines. It's classic Shackleton in so many ways, reaching back to canonical faves like 'Blood on My Hands' and his remix of Moderat's 'Rusty Nails', and yet it sounds as if the producer is furtively ushering us towards uncharted territory.

The direction is marked out even more visibly on 'The Unbeliever's Pulse' when Shackleton interrupts hard swung, hollow thuds with synthetic sweeps and swooshes - analog pulses and haunted drones that sound as if they've been snatched from Conrad Schnitzler's archives. There's a trace of vintage UKG in there somewhere (think Wookie or Groove Chronicles), but Shackleton upsets the rhythm with decaying dub echoes. Where Shackleton's earliest uptempo experiments were guided by the rapid momentum of bass music and his omnivorous interest in spiritual jazz, industrial music (particularly Muslimgauze) and global psychedelia, 'Euphoria Bound' folds in on itself, assessing a catalogue that now covers the length and breadth of his passions. There are few producers who manage to keep up their levels for quite so long, and even fewer who can refresh their palate so flawlessly.

items.body:
Posthumous reminder of MF Doom’s landmark classic, following the late, great MC’s death at the end of 2020 - with 11 tracks of bonus material.

A staple of our listening diet upon release in 2004 (probably preceded or followed by a listen to his ‘Special Blends volumes), ‘MM….Food’ still stands up among the greatest and most coveted hip hop albums of our time. Beats to bars, it’s a peerless example of Daniel Dumile Thompson’s MF Doom alias, playing out as a sort of stoned comic book fantasy voiced by a cartoon supervillain, literally inspired by Marvel Comics’ Doctor Doom, whose moniker sounds a bit like MF’s real middle name.  

The album oscillate between Doom’s mind-boggling metaphoric wordplay and his signature instrumentals, adapting the golden era ‘90s style of sampledelic collage and rugged rhymes to his singular purpose, and making a marked step on from his earlier work as Zev Love X with the legendary KMD. By choice or osmosis there’s probably a whole generation of headz who’ve committed the bars of ‘MM….Food’ to memory, and we can only recommend a refresher session right here if you’re rusty. Packing bags of nostalgia and vibes for days, it’s a true evergreen.

items.body:
Deepchord producer Rod Modell’s fruitful binds with Silentes’ 13 series yields its lushest outing yet, following in the glistening wake of Gigi Masin & Taka Noda jams to this elemental bliss out.

‘Grotto Of The Sun’ limns a metaphorical and physical thawing of Modell’s sound, in suit with the natural processes described on his ‘Frequencies in the Fog’ and ‘Northern Michigan Snowstorms’ albums. Exquisitely textured recordings of running water and birdsong are recombined with synthetic sound sources and diffused into a pair of durational tapestries that settle dead easy on the mind.

The presence of syrupy subbass lets you know we’re still in Modell’s hands, umbilically tied to dub techno, but it’s all much closer to the intentions of Japanese environmental ambient and adjacent new age in its esoteric outlook and contemplative outlook.

Shed plays to varied strengths on a rave-hungry double pack for Dekmantel, exerting signature, swingeing torque on heavy cuts of breakbeat techno-garage, trance and house.

The man-o-many-monikers settles on his OG alias for a haul of tuff meat motors speaking to his decades of skin in the game. He goes deep with the symphonic strings on a bustling breakbeat techno opener ‘Loot 25’, and percolates the drums with rude garage-techno suss in ‘Everybody’, and a simmering 2-step ace ‘Rave Predator’. Electro meets 2-step and lusher choral pads, kinda like Orbital, in ‘Password (Techno Mix)’, while recycling the same elements in full 4/4 flight on its trance mix, and his knack for proper, deep UK hardcore rufige comes into play on a standout ‘Double Scoop’, whereas ‘Taking You Home’ feels like one of his earliest Detroit techno-type winners, and ‘Rave Echoes’ teases that sound out into sublime, aerial tension with a whiff of Carl Craig & Derrick May’s ‘Relics’ about it.

Crackshot rap x club hybridiser Andrea Corradi splices dozens female spitters and mutant beats on ‘Outtakes’, the 2nd of his tapes for Reel Torque - Big RIYL DJ Screw, Rabit, Bobby Beethoven, Croww, Clams Casino, Hud Mo, Shadetek...

After his first volume sold out in a minute, Italian sound artist Andrea Corradi returns with a heat-seeking follow-up, shelling a 90 minute carousel of exclusive edits on tape, replete with a bonus 31 digital components for the DJs on an included download. It’s a rowdy cut ’n splice ram-raid that imagines; what would X rapper sound like on Y beat? The abundant results explore myriad permutations of this rudely unbalanced equation, from aggro jit paired with double speed fire, to Cerwin Vega-testing subs squashed with bitchiest bars, and genuine WTF‽ juxtapositions that go incredibly hard. 

The title ‘Outtakes’ knowingly undersells the prime material inside, which hits wider and just as rude as the ‘Ichinoya’ motherload which reached Mary Anne Hobbs’ BBC Radio 6 show and rinsed The White Hotel earlier this year. All the material lives up to expectations, firing from-the-hip mercurial fusions of underground, female rappers with leading-edge club ructions, with particular focus on mapping mutual, metric sweetspots between tunes that were never supposed to go together, but clearly work a treat. 

It’s effectively one of the canniest exercises in locating the mythical “3rd track” that we’ve heard in a hot minute, nailing the transitory pleasure of on-the-fly blends with a game sense of daring and rude empathy that rewards many happy returns in its spectrum of surprises - especially if you’ve had a keen ear on these pages over the years.

TIP!

items.body:
At this point you shouldn’t need any introduction to Liz Harris.. She’s got a few albums and splits under her belt now, but chances are the first time you came across her music was the stunning modern classic ‘Dragging A Dead Deer Up A Hill’, released back in 2008.

It was the distinct and singular blend of shimmering dreampop and tape-mangled noise that had just about anyone worth their salt in awe of her music, so you can imagine the hype surrounding this one. Ah, but then it’s not only one record is it? A I A is two full forty minute full-lengths, and rather than a traditional double, these are two distinct albums, each one with its own focus and style. ‘Alien Observer’ might be the more outwardly song-based of the two, and while the songs aren’t necessarily as clearly defined as those on ‘Dragging A Dead Deer Up A Hill’, they slowly and pointedly push up through Liz’s familiar, hazed layers . Her distinct tones are barely audible over the mudded harmonies, starting life as ghostly echoes, but the further you get into it, more clearly defined shapes start to emerge.

It's music that no doubt changes with each listen – you're left to fill in the gaps - and while we can hear the heaving breaths of the Cocteau Twins, The Red House Painters and This Mortal Coil wrenching themselves from somewhere, we'd probably come to a different conclusion on the next listen. ‘Alien Observer’ is a markedly different record from its predecessor, and comes across as a deeply thoughtful blend of the harrowing, sincere experiments of Liz’s early records and the sort of songwriting that lodged ‘Heavy Water’ in our collective memory back in 2008.

items.body:
Totally mesmerising ’70s Ghanaian highlife, licked with palmwine guitar and subtly in step with US soul as much as traditions rootsy sound, which made it a domestic bestseller at the time.

"A defining recording of the era, Sikyi Highlife bridges tradition and innovation at a pivotal moment in Ghanaian music. Deeply rooted in the classic 1950s–’60s highlife sound, K. Gyasi drew inspiration from the ancient sikyi drum-dance of the Akan people of southern Ghana, shaping the album’s rhythms around its distinctive pulse. The vocal arrangements echo the traditional Akan modal style, grounding the music firmly in Ghana’s cultural heritage. Yet Sikyi Highlife is equally forward-thinking. As electric guitars became standard in highlife during the 1960s, the 1970s ushered in further experimentation. The Noble Kings broke new ground as the first highlife guitar band to incorporate keyboards and a full horn section into their sound, expanding the genre’s sonic possibilities while retaining its rootsy spirit.

Gyasi’s approach was part of a broader indigenisation movement among Ghana’s electric highlife bands in the post-independence era. Inspired by the nation’s ‘African Personality’ ethos and reinforced by Afrocentric messages arriving from American soul and funk, artists began reclaiming traditional forms within modern arrangements. Contemporaries included Koo Nimo, who revived the older palmwine style, and drummer Nii Ashitey, whose Wulomei band pioneered a folklorised Ga highlife sound from 1973.

Like many musicians of his generation, Gyasi was a passionate supporter of Ghana’s independence movement. In 1963, he travelled as a musical ambassador alongside Ghana’s first president, Kwame Nkrumah, performing across North Africa and the USSR and carrying Ghanaian culture onto the world stage.

The Noble Kings’ mid-’70s line-up featured some of the country’s finest musicians, including guitarist Eric Agyeman (who led the band at the time), Thomas Frimpong on drums and vocals, Ernest Honny on organ, and bassist Ralph Karikari - who was renowned for his innovative technique of translating the rhythms and tonal language of the traditional talking drum onto electric bass.

Upon its original release, Sikyi Highlife became one of the biggest-selling albums of the 1970s for Essiebons, earning Gyasi the affectionate honorary title of “Dr” from his devoted fans. Today, the album remains an evergreen classic, still cherished across Ghana and beyond."

items.body:
Originally released in 1976 on Piero Umiliani’s own Sound Work Shop imprint, Drammi e Speranze -issued under the pseudonym Rovi - stands as a refined example of his late-period library work.

"Performed by a compact string ensemble and subtly augmented by piano, Hammond organ, Eminent organ, and Rhodes, the album unfolds through a series of classically-informed compositions where melody takes center stage. Each piece is concise, evocative, and purpose-built - reflecting the functional yet highly expressive nature of Italian library music at its peak.

Conceptually, the record is structured in two contrasting halves: the first side explores themes of optimism and resolution, while the second delves into darker, more introspective territories, mirroring the emotional duality suggested by its title (Tragedies and Hopes). Long overlooked outside specialist circles, Drammi e Speranze is here presented for the first time ever on vinyl reissue, newly remastered to highlight the depth and tonal richness of Umiliani’s arrangements. This release celebrates 100 years since the birth of Piero Umiliani, honoring the enduring legacy of a composer whose work continues to resonate across cinematic, library, and contemporary sample-driven music."

Tarantino muse, Japanese actress and singer, Meiko Kaji’s 1974 album is given the reissue stardust treatment on its first new edition in 50+ years.

“Wewantsounds is delighted to continue its extensive reissue program of Meiko Kaji's early discography, originally released by Teichiku Records in Japan between 1972 and 1974. The Quentin Tarantino muse—famous for her starring roles in Lady Snowblood and Stray Cat Rock—was also a gifted singer. Otoko Onna Kokoro No Aika is another collection of superb cinematic songs featuring Kaji's signature mix of Japanese Pop and Groove, backed by lush, atmospheric orchestrations. This includes her rendition of "Tokyo Nagare Mono," the theme song for Seijun Suzuki's cult 1966 film Tokyo Drifter. This reissue features the original artwork and a eight-page insert with new liner notes by Hashim Kotaro Bharoocha, who interviewed Meiko Kaji for the occasion.”

items.body:
Jim O'Rourke and Jos Smolders team up again with the follow up to their first collaboration, Additive Inverse from 2021.

"Over a period of three years, both artists worked in sessions of a day, each in their own studio. The result is sometimes like a warm cloud of sounds, suddenly breaking up into a rhythmic, irregular pattern, after which it dives into introverted mindsets. The music is in constant flux.

The project followed the same workflow, but this time Jim took the lead and kicked off with a salvo of sounds that he extracted from his Kyma System. Both Jos and Jim were quite interested in the spectral character of sounds. Jim applied Kyma algorithms while Jos granulated his basic recordings. That way, textures are built, quite slowly moving from warm to gritty, from hard surfaces to deep sonic wells."

items.body:
First released by Drexciya’s James Stinson and Gerald Donald in 1999 after establishing a cult reputation via EPs and 12”s for UR, Rephlex and Warp, ’Neptune’s Lair’ was issued by Berlin’s Tresor to the acclaim of those in the know. Since James Stinson died in 2002, in subsequent years the album has become widely regarded as their definitive opus - a hugely sophisticated, imaginative piece of Afrofuturist sonic fiction embedded with deeply rooted politics.

As the album approaches its 23rd anniversary of release, it still holds the power to utterly transport us to other dimensions. Using the ocean and water as metaphor for deep space, and by extension a site of the unknown, where far-fetched (but not entirely unreasonable) ideas about slave babies thrown overboard on slave-trade routes evolved into futuristic, practically alien beings, Drexciya, much like Sun Ra and his Saturnian roots, formed a whole world unto themselves thru their music, track titles and Abdul Haqq’s artwork, creating a sort of holistic gesamtkunstwerk as rich in subtext and noumenal flights of fancy as the most cult comic books or underground animation and cinema. 

In context of the very late ‘90s, when ‘Neptune’s Lair’ was issued, these ideas were necessary and important, as the electronic paradigm had been largely whitewashed by labels, promoters and DJs who either didn’t understand, or didn’t want to understand, the roots of the worldwide dance phenomenon that cropped up a decade prior - one mostly generated by PoC based in urban US cities. It’s perhaps as important as ever to acknowledge Drexciya’s origins and intent, to historically hold their work up to the rest of the field as waves of new, plugged in dancers become enthralled by their Hi-Tech Sci-Fi.

Classic.

items.body:
High impact, sound designer-sculpted industrial techno drama by french engineer-artist Franck Vigroux, shifting away from Mika Vainio worship to a more personalised sound, comparable to Mondkopf, an amped up JMJ, or Thomas Bangaltar’s ‘Irreversible’ OST.

“French composer and sound artist Franck Vigroux returns to raster with a new album called »Sonnailles«, set for release this spring.Conceived as a sequence-driven work, »Sonnailles« unfolds through a series of tightly structured musical passages interspersed with fragments of voices that appear within the compositions like ghostly presences. These vocal shards drift through the sonic landscape, punctuating Vigroux’s dense electronic textures and amplifying the album’s sense of tension and movement.

At the heart of the project lies a deliberate contrast: the collision of raw, almost primitive sonic force with an underlying sense of compositional sophistication. Vigroux crafted the music with an ear for immediacy and physical impact, exploring how rough textures and driving rhythms can coexist with intricate sound design.The album was also inspired by two unusual invitations that pushed the artist beyond his typical performance environments: a rock and punk festival in France and a series of techno club performances in China. These contexts led Vigroux to imagine music whose primary purpose was to move bodies on the dance floor — an approach that marks a new direction in his work.

For Vigroux, the challenge was particularly compelling. Alongside his musical practice, he frequently collaborates with dancers and stages multidisciplinary performances known for their radical physicality. With this new album, he brings those parallel worlds together, completing a circle in his ongoing exploration of the relationship between sound and the moving body — where composition, rhythm, and physical motion converge.”

items.body:
Belgian avant-pop outfit Sergeant return to STROOM with a second album and a new member. RIYL Milan W, Total Blue or Animal Collective.

Since 2023's self-titled debut album, movie bro Benjamin Cools and actor Ferre Marnef have invited a new artist into the fold. The project was initially conceived as a live band, so the additional personnel just allows Sergeant to spread their creative wings; 'Symbols' is a more complicated record than its predecessor, packed out with byzantine arrangement and layered compositions, but it's also tighter. There's a feeling that their influences - '80s DIY pop, krautrock and post-punk - have been more fluidly lashed together this time around and Marnef's voice sounds more assured bedded in his collaborators' woozy, sometimes spiky productions. 

If their last record was "DJ Shadow in reverse", made from collaged elements and half-songs, 'Symbols' is a suite of proper compositions that dissolve as they play out, with tempos fluctuating and components mutating and vaporizing as Marnef sings. It's pop music that's engineered with Martin Hannett's ear for wacked-out production - fans of Ariel Pink (before he went full fash) or Panda Bear's 'Person Pitch' should investigate without delay.

It doesn't take long to tune into the mood of "Universe In Blue"'s chilly title track. With Sun Ra on his "intergalactic space organ" accompanied by sparse, barely-audible drums, Kwame Hadi on trumpet and John Gilmore on horn, it's a longing blues improvisation that gets to the gooey core of Ra's appeal. This is the sound of Alabama's deep sadness, channelled through ancient and modern technologies that heave through the almost 15-minute composition as Ra leads with monastic charm, lashing the church to the juke joint. June Tyson brings a confident, blown-out vocal performance to 'When the Black Man Ruled This Land' (conspicuously truncated to 'Blackman' on the original issue), emoting over Ra's organ blasts. It's the album's most upfront cut, allowing cracks of sunlight to part the darkness for just a second.

'In a Blue Mood' meanwhile continues where the title track left off, centering Ra's emotional organ jamming over skeletal drums, allowing the texture and timbre of the electric organ the space to cough and splutter emotionally. Anyone who already knows the record will no doubt be interested to pick thru the two additions: 'Discipline 27-II' and 'Intergalactic Research'. Both have been released before but not collected with this exact material, and both were recorded in 1972, so while they hover around a different mood - this ain't sedate organ blues - they capture Ra in the same creative tidal wave.

items.body:
Budapest-based concept label, Blue Sun launches their new line of vinyl focused releases, aimed primarily on DJs and collectors: the Blue Series. A counterpart to the Orange Series launched in 2025 that showcases a more upbeat side of the label, the new collection presents a darker, more experimental, and introspective musical vision.

"The first release in the Blue Series is a six-track EP by Budapest based multimedia artist, Virág Réti. Choosing her legal name as her artist persona (“Flower of the Meadow" in Hungarian) also with the track titles capturing the folk names of local fauna, Peremidő evokes the artist's innate connection to nature as a place of refuge from the noise of Eastern European urban life.

The EP’s motifs point back to early memories of sitting by a river, simply observing time flowing by. The arc of the songs follow the passage of a day, beginning with the hesitant sounds of early morning, gradually moving on toward more defined, rhythm-driven forms. As the airy textures slowly give way to structure and percussion comes to the forefront, the sense of direction becomes clearer, letting moments of gentle disorder and unexpected sounds to surface.

Virág previously appeared on the label’s Blue Sun VA II compilation with her track Bíbic. Since launching her ambient music project in the fall of 2024, she has become one of the promising newcomers in the Hungarian experimental electronic music scene. Her debut EP, Minden Ami Megmaradt (All That Remains), was released last November as the final offering of temporary nites label (2023–2025). She is also the founder and organizer of the Budapest-based experimental electronic event series Still Places."

items.body:
Chicago quartet U.S. Maple's best album, 'Acre Thrills' is an American avant-rock masterpiecce that torches established formula unremittingly, singlehandedly creating music that's never quite been repeated - or bettered. Essential listening FFO Gastr del Sol, Hella, even black midi.

By the time U.S. Maple released 'Acre Thrills' in 2001, they'd already proved what they needed to prove, building up a so-called "math rock" sound out of the bones of Captain Beefheart's deconstructed 'Trout Mask Replica' and tearing it apart on the fly. And even when they brushed with the college rock underground's top levels, opening for Pavement and potentially glomming onto a completely new audience, they stuck to their guns, getting weirder rather than sanding down their sharp edges. This album isn't as dark as its predecessor by any means (we're gonna blame 'Talker' producer Michael Gira for that one), but it's more delicately arranged somehow - a perfectly imperfect lattice of angular, xenharmonic riffs and interlock'd polyrhythms that still somehow manage to couch vocalist Al Johnson's almost inhuman groans and monologues. His delivery's like Marmite, undoubtedly, but it's another element of the U.S. Maple sound that makes them impossible to properly replicate - despite bands endlessly trying ever since.

Although 'Acre Thrills' almost relishes its own knottiness, it's packed with moments that sound almost welcoming, at least to us. Opener 'Ma Digital' is surprisingly soft, Johnson's voice just a low hum underneath Mark Shippy and Todd Rittman's pretty breezy, almost hummable riffs, and if you didn't know better, you might confuse 'Babe' for a bluesier post-hardcore experiment, like Karate through a blender. By 'Untitled' though, their claws are fully on show with an instrumental that deconstructs itself as it plays through, falling apart into run-out-groove noise that's supposed to make you question what you're listening to. And when the album jolts back to life with 'Obey Your Concert', it's bolder, trickier and edgier, with Johnson veering from David Thomas to David Bowie in a matter of seconds. In the wrong hands, this kind of studied, hyper-technical grandstanding would be like nails on a chalkboard, so it's genuinely shocking that U.S. Maple managed to make it sound not just effortless but enduringly edgy. It's not noodly prog, it's grinding, painful, urgent music that understands the all-important polarity of blues, rock and all its variants.

items.body:
Italian ambient maestro Gigi Masin returns to his happy place on 'Movement', following 2020's 'Calypso' with a record that surveys a quarter century of vintage back room sounds, pulling from kosmische, new age, early techno, glitch and balearic house. 

For the last few years, Masin has been busy with a litany of collaborations, working with Jonny Nash and Young Marco as Gaussian Curve, with dub techno OG Rod Modell on 2023's 'Red Hair Girl at Lighthouse Beach and with jazz pianist Greg Foat on a ruck of soundtrack-y downtempo material. In fact it's been years since his last solo release; the Apollo-released 'Calypso' came out six years ago and 'Movement' appears to pick up where it left off. The waterlogged, sun-bleached concept is all but gone, but the sounds, cherry-picked from across the downtempo spectrum, are very much in keeping. 

Opener 'Bed on Mars' is classic Masin and should appeal to fans of his cult 1986 breakout 'Wind', the long-overlooked album that featured 'Clouds', that new age/ambient anthem that relaunched his career after it was sampled by both To Rococo Rot and Björk. It's a fleeting moment, but it's packed to the brim with the good stuff: humid post-Vangelis pads, synthetic choirs and reflecting pools of reverb. And the atmosphere's pierced by loping rhythms almost immediately; 'Lost' matches its elasticated brass moans with a low-slung beat and then 'The Age of Sampling' appears to hark back to the Fairlight era, conjuring up an industrial soundscape with jerky low-bitrate drum hits, dialog samples and inclement textures that sound like they belong on Black Rain's 'Neuromancer' soundtrack.

The title track is even more surprising, a slippery 120bpm house groover that sounds as if it's been precision engineered for hazy sunrises, with sax wails and vocal pads ducking behind its rubbery beats. If that sounds a bit much, then there's a few quieter spells, like the piano-led 'UMI' and the Shuttle358-inspired closer 'Fifteen', but you can tell that for Masin, "ambient" doesn't mean beatless. The highlight, 'Deception Dance', sounds like classic beardy back-room techno, even - the sort of twitchy biz Carl Craig used to engineer when he was still moonlighting as 69.

items.body:
Thessa Torsing (aka upsammy) and drum deity Valentina Magaletti consolidate their intentions on 'Seismo', rustling up an illusory combo of artificial and live sonics - properly RIYL early Squarepusher, Matmos or Mira Calix.

When roles are so clearly demarcated, it can be hard to keep things challenging. Magaletti's a percussionist first and foremost, while Torsing is clearly happiest working on the DAW or behind the decks, but neither artist wanted their collaboration to be quite so predictable. So they figured out a way to make their respective roles  a little more complicated; after recording Magaletti's acoustic parts in Amsterdam's labyrinthine Rijksmuseum, Torsing decided to compliment them with digital percussion - mallet-style instruments that mimic or at least harmonize with Magaletti's elements. The result is a puzzling assembly of samples, sequences and breathless improvisations that injects some much-needed energy into the '90s Artificial Intelligence scaffolding Torsing has been respraying for the last few years.

Opener 'It comes to an end' yanks us back to Squarepusher's beardy jazz crossover era, or Matmos's ace early electroacoustic experiments. But Torsing and Magaletti keep things fresh, offsetting their ornate biomechanical flurries with Reich-ian minimalist phrases and xenharmonic prangs that keep us on our toes. It's unashamedly percussive material and yet plays like a sequence of lullabies, its virtuosic drumwork (just check the smoove editing on 'Superimposed') almost inevitably offset by music box chimes or cloudy, dreamlike pads. The other element that sets the duo apart is the vocals; peppered throughout the album are dialog snippets that keep things confusing, countering their surreal twangs and iceberg-cracking whirrs with alien whispers that only just permeate the membrane.

Is there even a voice on 'Hyperlocalize', or is it just our imagination? We can't be quite sure. But the garbled syllables are more audible on 'Mementoes', sandwiched between soothing, rubbery lead synths and hallucinated xylophones. Needless to say, if you're into anything from Plaid to Midori Takada, this'll be worth a closer listen.

items.body:
Returning after a 13 year absence, Boards of Canada's vision of hell isn't exactly surprising, swapping out the magic hour guitars of 'The Campfire Headphase' and the tired Carpenter-isms of 'Tomorrow's Harvest' for jagged distortions, dialog snippets and uneasy religious symbolism.

It can't be easy for Mike Sandison and Marcus Eoin; as soon as they cracked the code with 'Music Has the Right to Children' in 1998, their home-brewed signature sound - tape-warped, reverb-soaked monosynths, stuttering dialog samples and thumping MPC-breaks - became a sort of meme, regurgitated by a wave of bedroom musicians so frequently that the original references became fully hollow. Those early records were great because they sounded so unique, marking a landscape littered with post-'Chiastic Slide' crunches and choppy AFX-ian amens with new channels of thought. Just go back to their shadowy 'Twoism', 'Hi Scores', or that Mask 500 cover of 'Midas Touch' -  there was nowt else like it. By the time we got to 'The Campfire Headphase', a comparatively sunny, guitar-led misstep that arrived a few years later and then 2013's 'Tomorrow's Harvest' -  it all felt like diminishing returns.

'Inferno''s mysterious VHS rollout also felt overly familiar - and if you're gonna tease, the payoff best be worth it. Sadly, first single 'Prophecy At 1420 MHz' was damp and old fashioned, lumpen with boxy '80s drums and awkward prog rock synths - the signs didn't look good. Heard as a whole though, 'Inferno' hangs together pretty well. The brothers do a good job of laying out a vision of hell that's intricately connected to their well-worn source material: the lost future that was promised to wide-eyed 1970s kids raised on color TV, welfare and action figures. Back then, religious cults and street cranks were screaming of damnation, convincing weakened minds that judgement was coming while the Vietnam War raged - real hell was on the doorstep all along. And it's hard not to hear Boards' blend of seemingly old-fashioned religious symbolism (the Hare Krishna chants, chopped-up divinity school lectures and guided meditations) as an indirect reference to the wars raging right now. Certainly, it's their darkest album in years; not the aesthetic darkness of 'Tomorrow's Harvest', either. 'Father and Son', with its eerie Abrahamic symbolism, feels like an American Gothic reflection of Leslie Nielsen's comparatively benign narrations on 'Geogaddi', while 'Memory Death' feels like Boards actively sending off their own patented brand of hauntology with the EKG blip to prove it.

Throughout the record, BoC appear to juxtapose a cultural concept of hell with their own aesthetic responses, balancing dystopian robot voices with squelchy acid gurgles on the excellent 'The Word Becomes Flesh' and Bobby Beausoleil-style chiming strings on 'Blood in the Labyrinth'.  'The Process', meanwhile, offers a late-stage vision of aviation hell, a 'Langoliers'-style horror cue that neatly precedes the saccharine vintage BoC hit of 'You Retreat in Time and Space'. Perhaps unsurprisingly, it's these beatless moments that really hold things together - maybe they should have just leaned into it and done a full length of those vignettes. Still, 'Inferno' has its moments.

items.body:
By Sammy Stein

Apeiron is the new project by double bassist and composer Jacopo Ferrazza and pianist and composer Sebastian Marino, released on CD and digital formats on Teal Dreamers Factory.

The press release says that on the album, ‘double bass, piano, and experimental electronics coexist without hierarchies, generating a sound environment in which timbral origins often become indistinguishable.’ But a listen reveals this is not quite true. The timbral origins of the instruments and the electronics are distinguishable, with the deep body of the bass providing a definitive, characteristic timbre that no electronics can replicate. What does happen, however, is that the sounds of the double bass as it is played with the bow, or pizzicato, the piano, and the electronics of the mini-Moog, synth, and Hammond, intermingle and entwine, creating an effect akin to multi-instrumental music, yet the nuances and sonic elements of bass and piano are discernible. The electronics act as an extension of the instrumental dialogue through which the two musicians expand the possibilities of listening and interaction. Interestingly, the music circles around a poem:

Close Your Eyes
And Step Beyond the Edge of What You Know
There Is a Flame Inside You
Ancient Patient Waiting
It Has No Name
It Has No Beginning
It Is the Breath Before the First Word Was Spoken
Feel It
Rising Softly Through Your Spine
Like Liquid Gold in the Dark
You Are Not the Body
You Are Not the Thought
You Are the Pulse Beneath the Silence
Let the World Dissolve
Let the Noise Fall Away
There Is Only This Moment
This Warmth This Sacred Unfolding
Whisper to Yourself: I Remember
Because You Do
You Have Always Known
And Now the Flame Awakens

Each track is titled as a line from the poem, so both the concept and the music create a whole. The music is divided into two macro blocks, the first ten tracks form Epanastasi (Repetition) and the second eleven form Oneiro (Dreams). The title Apeiron is Greek and means boundless or undefined, and is apt for the music, which sees the musicians create landscapes of sound ranging from gentle whispers of entreaty to forceful, expressive density. Each track forms its own encapsulated narrative yet is linked to the rest of the music in subtle ways. The relentless repetition of the piano note on ‘Close Your Eyes’, surrounded by experimental, explorative sounds, is intense, yet somehow compelling as it leads to the short, intense forty-six seconds of ‘And Step beyond The Edge of What You Know’, which melds itself into ‘There is A Flame Inside You’, which feels almost ecclesiastical with its organ lines and vocal electronics. The bass swells in glorious tones out of the generous mix of sound, and the piano gently calms the madness that appears to be present in the music. You can almost feel the intention of Ferrazza, which, he describes as creating music, “where bass, piano and electronics function as a single evolving system.” There is a sense of the instruments feeding each other ideas, snippets to develop and run with, or shifts in mind and direction.

The lines of the poem as track titles offer concepts but rarely fit the atmosphere of the track to which they are assigned – but here the poem is a tool to weld the music together and give a route to follow, whether that is strictly or using diverse routes. The music unfolds, it is dynamic and, in places, terrifyingly beautiful in its fragility. Like on ‘Ancient Patient Waiting,’ where Ferrazza’s bass rises, its voice a gorgeous solo, its timbre palpable, the sounds swirling around the wooden body of the instrument and emerging smooth and warm, or the gentleness of both piano and bass on ‘It Has No Name.’

There are several standout tracks, including ‘It Has No Beginning,’ with its otherworldly atmosphere, which merges seamlessly into ‘It Is The Breath Before The First Word Was Spoken’ where deep electronics and synth lines give this a seventies prog vibe.

Both musicians have classical groundings, and this reveals itself in their harmonies and naturally evolving chordal episodes on some tracks, including the dynamic and emotive ‘Feel It.’

I found nothing but good in this music; the evolution of sounds is dynamic and interesting, so that even someone who is not fond of synth or Hammond found it incredibly engaging. The minds of these two musicians come together through their instruments to make music that is astonishing in the many ways it manages to engage the listener.

Both musicians have space to shine – like the bass rising on ‘Like Liquid Gold In The Dark’ and ‘You Are Not The Body,’ where Ferrazza finds endless elements of the instrument, or the piano on ‘You Are Not The Thought.’

Some tracks are an entity of their own, while others merge into each other, broken not by a change of tempo but a change of direction, slight then deliberate and divergent. Like from ‘You Are the Pulse Beneath the Silence’ to’ Let the World Dissolve.’

The second block of tracks (dreams) seems like one narrative, with different chapters, the music a changing dialogue. There are more electronic sounds in this block, and on ‘Whisper to Yourself I Remember,’ there is a sense of a hellscape as voices and strange electronic background sounds make the music rather than instruments.

Interestingly enough, truculent piano, swooping bass, and weird electric sounds work a treat, like on ‘You Have Always Known.’ The final track sees a return to piano and bass playing at its best and most expressive.

This is a different step, as Ferrazza says, from his previous work. The album was fully improvised and recorded in a single session with no editing. The music unfurls through listening, tension, silence, and real-time transformation, moving between free improvisation and a more textural, electroacoustic space.

Ferrazza said he felt this might resonate with my interest in exploratory and boundary-crossing music, and he was right, but this music will resonate with many listeners because it is energetic when it needs to be, quiet when this is called for, and the music seems to follow an exquisite rhythm that somehow is defined and sits beautifully in the mind of the listener.

It is a testimony to how good musical dialogue becomes when musicians have a long association, such as the fifteen years of working together behind Ferrazza and Marino. I cannot recommend this album more.
